VIDEO.title: Matthew 14:1-21 – You Missed the REAL Meaning Behind Jesus Feeding the 5,000!
VIDEO.series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)

hand: They all ate and were satisfied.
SUMMARY: The teacher reads Matthew 14:1-21. Herod the tetrarch hears about Jesus and thinks John the Baptist has risen from the dead. Matthew then tells, as a flashback, how Herod had John arrested over Herodias and beheaded him at a birthday feast. When Jesus hears, He withdraws by boat to a desolate place, has compassion on the crowds, and feeds five thousand men, besides women and children, with five loaves and two fish.
The episode opens with Mark 8, where Jesus asks the disciples how many baskets they picked up and says, 'Do you not yet understand?' (Mark 8:21). Something about the numbers was a lesson they missed.

Matthew calls Herod 'the king' just as he acts most cowardly (14:9), which the video reads as irony. Herod's fear that John had risen shows he believed in a resurrection, as the Pharisees did and the Sadducees did not (Acts 23:8).

The video reads the numbers as symbols: five for the Torah, two for the tablets, seven for completeness, twelve for the tribes, a thousand for the full community of God's people (Deuteronomy 7:9). Jesus takes the complete law, rightly interpreted and fulfilled, gives it to His disciples, and they feed God's people until all are satisfied, with twelve baskets left over.
With the desolate place and the bread, Jesus shows He is the prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15). The lesson: Jesus and His teaching are more than sufficient to satisfy the needs of God's people.
QUOTES: He's not acting like a king at all in this moment.
Jesus and his teaching is more than sufficient to satisfy the needs of God's people.
In one fell swoop, Jesus is showing that he is the new Moses.

method.p: The teacher uses number symbolism because Jesus Himself asks about the baskets (Mark 8:19-21). He also warns that we should be very cautious about using this method today.

HEROD.title: He withdrew, and He had compassion

src.text: Now when Jesus heard about John, He withdrew from there in a boat to a desolate place by Himself; and when the crowds heard of this, they followed Him on foot from the cities. And when He went ashore, He saw a large crowd, and felt compassion for them and healed their sick.

lines.text: Jesus withdraws again, as He did in 12:15. Even so, when He sees the crowds He has compassion, as when He saw them 'like sheep without a shepherd' (9:36).

The video lists symbolic meanings: one for God, two for the two tablets, five for the Torah, seven for completeness, twelve for the tribes of Israel, a thousand for the full community of God's people. It calls this gematria and says the list is not exhaustive.
Why would numbers carry meaning? The video says Hebrew thought is concrete, not abstract: ask a first-century Jew to describe God and he will say God is a rock, a fortress, a shepherd.

src.text: You shall know therefore that Yahweh your God, He is God, the faithful God, who keeps His covenant and His lovingkindness to a thousand generations with those who love Him and keep His commandments;

lines.text: God does not quit after the thousandth generation: the thousand stands for the full community of His people. Five thousand, then, is the full community of those who follow the books of Moses.

NUMBERS.title: Five loaves, two fish, twelve baskets

src.text: And ordering the crowds to sit down on the grass, He took the five loaves and the two fish, and looking up toward heaven, He blessed the food. And breaking the loaves, He gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds, and they all ate and were satisfied. They picked up what was left over of the broken pieces, twelve full baskets.

lines.text: Five loaves (the Torah) and two fish (the tablets) make seven: the complete law. Jesus takes it, rightly interpreted and fulfilled by His own righteousness, and gives it to His disciples, who feed God's people.
All are satisfied from those seven pieces, and twelve baskets are left over, one for each tribe of Israel.

NUMBERS.title: He sat down, and He tested Philip

src.text: Then Jesus went up on the mountain, and there He was sitting down with His disciples. Now the Passover, the feast of the Jews, was near. Therefore Jesus, lifting up His eyes and seeing that a large crowd was coming to Him, *said to Philip, “Where should we buy bread, so that these people may eat?” And this He was saying to test him, for He Himself knew what He was going to do.

lines.text: Jesus is sitting, the posture of a teacher, and Passover is near. The meal is a teaching moment, a meal tied to the story of the Exodus.
Luke places these events near Bethsaida (Luke 9:10), on the edge of the Jewish region, bordering the Decapolis, where Jesus will feed the four thousand (15:32-39).

left.text: “Yahweh your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you, from your brothers; you shall listen to him.

right.text: Therefore when the people saw the sign which He had done, they were saying, “This is truly the Prophet who is to come into the world.”

lines.text: In one fell swoop, the video says, Jesus shows He is the new Moses, the one Moses said would come and speak God's words to God's people. John records that the crowd drew that very conclusion.

src.text: Then Yahweh said to Moses, “Behold, I will rain bread from heaven for you; and the people shall go out and gather a day’s portion every day, that I may test them, whether or not they will walk in My law.

lines.text: Even the desolate place echoes the Exodus, when God fed His people in the wilderness. The disciples say, 'This place is desolate' (14:15).
In Exodus the bread was a test of whether Israel would 'walk in My law'; in John, Jesus tests Philip (John 6:6).

src.text: And his attendant said, “What, will I give this before one hundred men?” But he said, “Give them to the people that they may eat, for thus says Yahweh, ‘They shall eat and have some left over.’” So he gave it before them, and they ate and had some left over, according to the word of Yahweh.

lines.text: Not in the video: Elisha fed a hundred men with twenty loaves and had some left over. Jesus feeds thousands with five.
Jesus and His teaching are more than sufficient to satisfy the needs of God's people. When the disciples let that sink in, they will see they already have everything they need in Jesus.
The disciples must still be fed by Him, by the power of the Holy Spirit, before they can feed others: 'you give them something to eat!' (14:16).

TERMS.def: Ruler of a quarter, a lesser title than king; Herod Antipas ruled Galilee and Perea.
Saying one thing to point to its opposite: Matthew calls Herod 'the king' just as he acts like a coward.
As the video uses it, attaching deeper meaning to numbers. Strictly, gematria computes the number values of letters in words.
A hint back to an Old Testament passage.
A wilderness or lonely spot, recalling Israel's time in the desert.
The one Moses promised would speak God's words (Deuteronomy 18:15-19).
Herod's fortress east of the Dead Sea, where Josephus says John was imprisoned and killed.

WORDS.gloss: To feel compassion, to be moved in one's inner parts. Look up: BDAG, σπλαγχνίζομαι.
Desolate, deserted; as a noun, wilderness.
To bless, to give thanks over food.
Prophet. Look up: BDB or HALOT, נָבִיא.

BACKGROUND.p: Josephus says that Herod sent John in chains to the fortress of Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea, and put him to death there, fearing his influence over the people. The hilltop fortress has been excavated, including a palace with a courtyard.

Herodias was a granddaughter of Herod the Great. She was first married to a half-brother of Antipas, whom the Gospels call Philip; she left him to marry Antipas, who divorced his own wife to marry her. Josephus names her daughter Salome.
Royal birthday feasts were lavish affairs for officials and leading men (Mark 6:21). A ruler's public oath before his guests was hard to break without losing face.
Barley loaves (John 6:9) were the bread of the poor, and dried or salted fish from the lake was a common relish. Magdala was known for processing fish.

DEBATES.h: How far to press the numbers?
DEBATES.p: Many readers see the twelve baskets as a sign for Israel, and the seven baskets of 15:37 as fullness. Assigning a meaning to every number (five for the Torah, two for the tablets) is less widely held; the teacher himself urges caution.
Luke points to Bethsaida (9:10), John to 'the other side of the Sea of Galilee' (John 6:1). The traditional site at Tabgha on the north-west shore dates to the Byzantine period.

DEBATES.h: Was Herod a believer in resurrection?
DEBATES.p: The video takes Herod's words at face value. Others read them as a guilty conscience speaking, or as popular superstition rather than settled belief.

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: The video says Bethsaida is named 'in both Luke and Mark, or excuse me, John's account.' Luke names Bethsaida (9:10); John's account of the feeding places it on 'the other side of the Sea of Galilee' (John 6:1), and Mark sends the disciples on to Bethsaida afterward (Mark 6:45).
What the video calls gematria is broader number symbolism. Gematria in the strict sense calculates the number values of letters and is attested in rabbinic writings later than the Gospels.
'Only approximately 8,000 words in the Hebrew language' refers to the vocabulary of the Hebrew Bible; later Hebrew has many more words.
Matthew is not alone in calling Herod 'the king': Mark calls him 'King Herod' throughout (Mark 6:14), so the irony is the video's reading of Matthew's choice.
The chart of number meanings is the video's own; the Bible does not give such a key.
The captions write 'Herodiius' for Herodias, 'Gamatria' for gematria, 'Bethida' for Bethsaida, 'Dicapus' for Decapolis, and 'Philillip' for Philip.

QUESTIONS: Why do you think Matthew tells John's death as a flashback right here?
Herod cared more about his oath and his guests than about doing right. Where do you feel pressure to save face?
Jesus withdrew to grieve, yet had compassion when the crowds came. What does that teach about Him?
What do you make of the number symbolism? Where would you be cautious?
'You give them something to eat!' What do you have that Jesus could multiply for others?
Is Jesus and His teaching enough for you? Where are you looking elsewhere to be satisfied?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: The lesson, stated plainly: Jesus and His teaching are more than sufficient to satisfy the needs of God's people. When the disciples really let that sink in, and they haven't yet, they will recognize that they have everything they need already in Jesus. Jesus takes the complete law, rightly interpreted and fulfilled by His own righteousness, gives it to His disciples, and they in turn feed those who come to Him; and when God's people eat Jesus' law, they are satisfied, with leftovers to spare. In one fell swoop Jesus shows that He is the new Moses, the one Moses said would come and speak God's words to God's people. We too need to come to Jesus by the power of the Holy Spirit to receive the lesson and to consume the meal He has prepared for us, because yes, this still teaches today.
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): read Mark 8:14-21 slowly. Jesus does not scold the disciples for forgetting bread; He asks whether they remember what He already did. Name one way He has already provided for you.

## The prophet like Moses
1. Deuteronomy 18:15-19: A prophet like Moses
   Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15, LSB): "“Yahweh your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you, from your brothers; you shall listen to him."
   The crowd (John 6:14, LSB): "Therefore when the people saw the sign which He had done, they were saying, “This is truly the Prophet who is to come into the world.”"
   (video) In one fell swoop, the video says, Jesus shows He is the new Moses, the one Moses said would come and speak God's words to God's people. John records that the crowd drew that very conclusion.
2. Exodus 16:4: Bread in a desolate place
   Exodus Exodus 16:4: "Then Yahweh said to Moses, “Behold, I will rain bread from heaven for you; and the people shall go out and gather a day’s portion every day, that I may test them, whether or not they will walk in My law." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Exodus+16:4
   (video) Even the desolate place echoes the Exodus, when God fed His people in the wilderness. The disciples say, 'This place is desolate' (14:15).
   [Background] In Exodus the bread was a test of whether Israel would 'walk in My law'; in John, Jesus tests Philip (John 6:6).
3. 2 Kings 4:42-44: Elisha's twenty loaves
   Also 2 Kings 4:43-44: "And his attendant said, “What, will I give this before one hundred men?” But he said, “Give them to the people that they may eat, for thus says Yahweh, ‘They shall eat and have some left over.’” So he gave it before them, and they ate and had some left over, according to the word of Yahweh." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=2+Kings+4:43-44
   [Background] Not in the video: Elisha fed a hundred men with twenty loaves and had some left over. Jesus feeds thousands with five.
4. The lesson: More than sufficient
   (video) Jesus and His teaching are more than sufficient to satisfy the needs of God's people. When the disciples let that sink in, they will see they already have everything they need in Jesus.
   (video) The disciples must still be fed by Him, by the power of the Holy Spirit, before they can feed others: 'you give them something to eat!' (14:16).

## Key people
- Herod the tetrarch: Fears John has risen; calls for John's head to save face before his guests. [Background] Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, ruled Galilee and Perea from 4 BC to AD 39.
- Herodias: Herod's brother's wife; she prompts her daughter to ask for John's head. [Background] Mark says she held a grudge against John and wanted to put him to death (Mark 6:19).
- The daughter of Herodias: Dances at Herod's birthday and asks for the head on a platter. [Background] Unnamed in the Gospels; Josephus names Herodias's daughter Salome.
- John the Baptist: Imprisoned and beheaded for saying, 'It is not lawful for you to have her.' [Background] The Law forbade taking a brother's wife while the brother lived (Leviticus 18:16).
- Philip: Tested by Jesus: 'Where should we buy bread?' [Background] Philip was from Bethsaida (John 1:44).
- The disciples: Told, 'you give them something to eat!' They distribute the bread. [Background] Mark has them return from their own mission just before (Mark 6:30).

## Places [Background]
- Bethsaida (named in the video): Luke places the feeding near 'a city called Bethsaida' (Luke 9:10), just east of where the Jordan enters the lake.
- Capernaum: Jesus' base on the north shore.
- Tabgha: The traditional site of the feeding, with a church of the multiplication; the Gospels point instead toward Bethsaida.
- Tiberias: Herod Antipas' capital on the lake; Herod's court is where the story begins.

## Key terms
- Tetrarch: Ruler of a quarter, a lesser title than king; Herod Antipas ruled Galilee and Perea. [Background]
- Irony: Saying one thing to point to its opposite: Matthew calls Herod 'the king' just as he acts like a coward.
- Gematria: As the video uses it, attaching deeper meaning to numbers. Strictly, gematria computes the number values of letters in words.
- Remez: A hint back to an Old Testament passage.
- Desolate place: A wilderness or lonely spot, recalling Israel's time in the desert.
- Prophet like Moses: The one Moses promised would speak God's words (Deuteronomy 18:15-19).
- Machaerus: Herod's fortress east of the Dead Sea, where Josephus says John was imprisoned and killed. [Background]

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- Machaerus: Josephus says that Herod sent John in chains to the fortress of Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea, and put him to death there, fearing his influence over the people. The hilltop fortress has been excavated, including a palace with a courtyard.
- Herodias: Herodias was a granddaughter of Herod the Great. She was first married to a half-brother of Antipas, whom the Gospels call Philip; she left him to marry Antipas, who divorced his own wife to marry her. Josephus names her daughter Salome.
- Birthday banquets: Royal birthday feasts were lavish affairs for officials and leading men (Mark 6:21). A ruler's public oath before his guests was hard to break without losing face.
- Bread and fish: Barley loaves (John 6:9) were the bread of the poor, and dried or salted fish from the lake was a common relish. Magdala was known for processing fish.

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- How far to press the numbers? Many readers see the twelve baskets as a sign for Israel, and the seven baskets of 15:37 as fullness. Assigning a meaning to every number (five for the Torah, two for the tablets) is less widely held; the teacher himself urges caution.
- Where was the feeding? Luke points to Bethsaida (9:10), John to 'the other side of the Sea of Galilee' (John 6:1). The traditional site at Tabgha on the north-west shore dates to the Byzantine period.
- Was Herod a believer in resurrection? The video takes Herod's words at face value. Others read them as a guilty conscience speaking, or as popular superstition rather than settled belief.

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- The video says Bethsaida is named 'in both Luke and Mark, or excuse me, John's account.' Luke names Bethsaida (9:10); John's account of the feeding places it on 'the other side of the Sea of Galilee' (John 6:1), and Mark sends the disciples on to Bethsaida afterward (Mark 6:45).
- What the video calls gematria is broader number symbolism. Gematria in the strict sense calculates the number values of letters and is attested in rabbinic writings later than the Gospels.
- 'Only approximately 8,000 words in the Hebrew language' refers to the vocabulary of the Hebrew Bible; later Hebrew has many more words.
- Matthew is not alone in calling Herod 'the king': Mark calls him 'King Herod' throughout (Mark 6:14), so the irony is the video's reading of Matthew's choice.
- The chart of number meanings is the video's own; the Bible does not give such a key.
- The captions write 'Herodiius' for Herodias, 'Gamatria' for gematria, 'Bethida' for Bethsaida, 'Dicapus' for Decapolis, and 'Philillip' for Philip.

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. Why do you think Matthew tells John's death as a flashback right here?
2. Herod cared more about his oath and his guests than about doing right. Where do you feel pressure to save face?
3. Jesus withdrew to grieve, yet had compassion when the crowds came. What does that teach about Him?
4. What do you make of the number symbolism? Where would you be cautious?
5. 'You give them something to eat!' What do you have that Jesus could multiply for others?
6. Is Jesus and His teaching enough for you? Where are you looking elsewhere to be satisfied?

## Application
- (video) The lesson, stated plainly: Jesus and His teaching are more than sufficient to satisfy the needs of God's people. When the disciples really let that sink in, and they haven't yet, they will recognize that they have everything they need already in Jesus. Jesus takes the complete law, rightly interpreted and fulfilled by His own righteousness, gives it to His disciples, and they in turn feed those who come to Him; and when God's people eat Jesus' law, they are satisfied, with leftovers to spare. In one fell swoop Jesus shows that He is the new Moses, the one Moses said would come and speak God's words to God's people. We too need to come to Jesus by the power of the Holy Spirit to receive the lesson and to consume the meal He has prepared for us, because yes, this still teaches today.
- Study note (added): read Mark 8:14-21 slowly. Jesus does not scold the disciples for forgetting bread; He asks whether they remember what He already did. Name one way He has already provided for you.
